name: Face pulls / band pull-aparts
lead: Face pulls and band pull-aparts are upper-back exercises that train the rear deltoids, the muscles between the shoulder blades and the small rotator-cuff muscles that turn the arm outward. A face pull is usually done with a rope attachment on a cable stack set near head height, pulling toward the face with the elbows high [1]. A band pull-apart is done by holding a resistance band at arm's length in front of the chest and drawing the hands apart until the band touches the chest.

People in lifting and looksmaxxing circles use them to improve posture and shoulder shape. The deltoid forms the rounded contour of the shoulder [2], and stronger rear delts and mid-back muscles are said to pull the shoulders back, open the chest and give the shoulders a fuller look from the side and behind, which proponents say helps a V-taper and a more upright, taller-looking stance. The National Academy of Sports Medicine presents the face pull as a pulling exercise for correcting postural dysfunctions and improving shoulder health [1].

Both movements are light, low-load exercises commonly added to pressing-heavy training days. Barbell Medicine describes face pulls as an accessory that serious lifters use to offset heavy chest and front-shoulder training, noting that relatively light weights may give enough stimulus while limiting fatigue [3]. They are popular partly because they need little equipment: resistance bands are light and portable [4], and the cable version is found in most gyms.

chain: Trains rear delts, mid-back and rotator cuff
Shoulders sit further back and the upper back gains thickness
More upright posture and a fuller, wider-looking shoulder line
angle.text: Face pulls and band pull-aparts build the rear delts and upper-back muscles that hold the shoulders back. People use them alongside pressing work to balance the front of the shoulder and to stand and look more upright, with rounder shoulders from behind and the side.

infobox: Posterior deltoid, rhomboids; secondary middle trapezius, infraspinatus [1]

paras: The face pull is performed at a cable station with a rope handle at roughly eye height [1]. The lifter pulls the rope toward the face while spreading the hands apart and rotating the upper arms outward, finishing with the elbows high and the shoulder blades squeezed together. Variants use a band anchored to a rack or door instead of a cable.

The band pull-apart uses a loop or tube band held in both hands at shoulder height with straight arms. The hands move outward to the sides until the band reaches the chest, then return slowly. Resistance bands are colour-coded by resistance, and bands of different thickness change how hard the movement is [4].

NASM lists the posterior deltoid and rhomboid major and minor as primary muscles for the face pull, with the middle trapezius, infraspinatus and biceps as secondary muscles [1]. Wikipedia says the posterior fibres of the deltoid help extend the shoulder and contribute to external rotation alongside the infraspinatus and teres minor, and are used in rowing movements [2]. Barbell Medicine lists the traps, rhomboids and rotator cuff as additional muscles worked [3].

Upper crossed syndrome is the term for the combination of forward head posture and rounded shoulders; Wikipedia describes the middle and lower back support muscles, including the rhomboids and middle and lower trapezius, as becoming stretched and weak, and lists strengthening scapular retractors and stretching tight neck and shoulder muscles as typical approaches, while noting that parts of the article need more reliable references [5]. Face pulls and pull-aparts target those scapular retractors and rear delts, which is why posture routines commonly list them together with rows.

In appearance-focused communities the exercises are discussed under posture, shoulder width and the V-taper. Proponents say that well-developed rear delts add visible roundness and width to the shoulders when viewed from behind and at an angle, and that a stronger upper back makes it easier to stand with the shoulders back and the chest open.

Electromyography studies cited by Barbell Medicine found high posterior deltoid activity for the reverse pec deck compared with the seated row and incline lat pulldown; face pulls were not part of those studies, and the article cautions that differences in muscle activity do not reliably predict differences in muscle size or strength [3]. The same article says there is no data supporting a specific push-to-pull training ratio [3].

Because loads are light, the exercises are generally regarded as low-risk. Coaching guidance typically emphasises controlled movement and making sure other muscles do not take over so that the rear delts do the work [3]. People with shoulder pain or injury are commonly advised to check technique with a coach or clinician.

No studies found on face pulls or band pull-aparts for posture or shoulder appearance. A 2014 study cited on Wikipedia found similar strength gains from bench presses and band push-ups at similar stress levels, a finding about band training in general [4].

card.aka: Rope face pulls, band pull-aparts, rear delt pulls

quick.overview:
Face pulls and band pull-aparts are accessory exercises for the back of the shoulders and the upper back. They are done with a cable and rope or a simple resistance band.

People add them to training to pull the shoulders back, build rounder rear delts and stand more upright, which they say gives a wider, more athletic shoulder line.
quick.mechanism: The movements load the rear deltoids, the muscles between the shoulder blades and the outward-rotating rotator-cuff muscles, which balance the chest and front-shoulder work from pressing exercises.
quick.risks: Loads are light and the exercises are generally regarded as low-risk; guidance usually stresses controlled form, and people with shoulder pain are advised to seek individual advice.
